    pass

examples.explanation: The changes between neighboring readings are 5, 1, 6 and 1. Only 5 and 6 are bigger than 3.
A drop of 10 and a rise of 10 both count as swings.

approaches.name: single pass over neighboring pairs with a counter
build a separate list of all the changes, then count

steps.title: Clarify the input
steps.description: Pins down what happens with fewer than two readings, whether a change of exactly k counts, and whether drops count as well as rises.
look_for: mentions an empty list or a single reading
asks whether a change equal to k is a swing
hints: Before you start coding, is there anything about the input you'd want to pin down?
What should the answer be if there are zero readings, or only one?
Settle the tiny inputs and the exactly-k case before you write the loop.

steps.title: Compare neighbors
steps.description: Compares each reading with the one right before it, not with the first reading or the largest reading so far.
look_for: compares a reading with the previous one
says 'each reading against the one before it'
hints: Look at which two readings you're comparing on each step.
A swing happens between which two readings exactly?
Walk through the list once, comparing each reading with its direct neighbor.

steps.title: Count drops as well as rises
steps.description: Measures the size of each change regardless of direction, so a fall in temperature counts the same as a rise.
look_for: uses the absolute value of the difference
hints: Try your idea on a list where the temperature only goes down.
Would a fall of 10 degrees count as a swing in your code?
You care about the size of the change, not its direction. Think about absolute value.

steps.title: Use a strict comparison
steps.description: Counts a swing only when the change is strictly greater than k, so a change of exactly k is not counted.
look_for: tests or mentions a change exactly equal to k
hints: Check what your code does with a change that is exactly k.
The problem says 'more than k'. Does your comparison match that?
A change equal to k is not a swing, so the comparison has to be strict.

edge_cases.description: a change exactly equal to k
drops in temperature, including negative readings

common_mistakes.description: only counts rises and ignores drops
common_mistakes.symptom: fails when the temperature falls, for example [80, 70] with k = 3

common_mistakes.description: uses 'greater than or equal to' instead of 'greater than'
common_mistakes.symptom: counts changes of exactly k, for example [10, 13, 16, 19] with k = 3

common_mistakes.description: starts the loop at index 0 and compares the first reading with temps[-1]
common_mistakes.symptom: in Python this wraps around and compares the first reading with the last one, adding an extra swing

wrap_up_questions: What are the time and space complexity?
How would you change this if readings arrived one at a time from a live sensor?

origin_note: Original. Pattern: single pass over neighboring pairs.
